newsitem.title: USA: Demand driving U.S. industry rebound - Fed sources.
newsitem.headline: Demand driving U.S. industry rebound - Fed sources.

text.p: The U.S. manufacturing sector appears to be regaining speed after a strong inventory build-up in the first quarter, driven mostly by strong demand from product-starved consumers, Federal Reserve sources said.

"The sales-to-inventory ratio remains at a fairly low level, indicating that perhaps the big build-up in inventories (in the first quarter) has been accompanied by a build-up in sales at the national level," said a source at the Federal Reserve who asked not to be named.
"This does suggest that demand is driving this rebound in the manufacturing sector," the source added.
Recent data released by the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) showed its manufacturing activity index jumped sharply in May to 57.1 from 54.2 in April.
The report also showed a sharp rise in its new orders component to 64.2 from 57.9 in the previous month.
Policy makers and financial markets watch the new orders item closely because it is perceived to provide a forward-looking view of manufacturing activity.

Fed sources said one of the key questions at the central bank today is whether or not the economy will slow down to a more sustainable growth rate after the torrid 5.8 percent expansion seen in the first quarter.

"We're monitoring the economy very closely. We know the pace of growth has slowed somewhat early in the second quarter; we just don't know whether it's going to stay that way," said another Fed source, who also asked not to be named.
So is there a possibility that the economy will slow down by itself through the year?
"I think that is possible since many believed in a slower pace through this year. But it's still hard to tell at this point," the second Fed source said.
So far, local manufacturing surveys produced by regional Federal Reserve banks have given mixed signals.
Raymond Owens, a regional economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, said manufacturers in the fifth U.S. economic district appear to be upbeat about the future of their businesses.
"Manufacturers, at least in our district, are looking for this rebound to have a bit of a staying power over the next several months at the very least, perhaps longer," Owens said.

"Our survey for May is being compiled. I don't know what that will show, but I know that the level of activity showing up today nationally did show up over the last couple of months here as well," Owens added.
The fifth U.S. economic region encompasses the District of Columbia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia and most of West Virginia.

Ted Crone, assistant vice president and regional economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, said manufacturing activity in his district did not appear to show the same rebound seen in the national numbers.

"Our business outlook survey in May didn't show that kind of jump. So I was a little surprised that the NAPM actually went up ... For the last couple of months our survey has been down, which doesn't jibe with the NAPM survey," Crone said.
"I'd like to see another month of data before I drew a conclusion that industrial production is going to be gangbuster again," Crone added.
The Philadelphia Fed's index of business activity in the manufacturing sector fell to 1.6 in May from 5.7 in April.

Asked about the future outlook for the manufacturing in the region, Crone said that "the pattern for here on out is likely to be weakness here and weakness there despite overall growth in the nation."
The Philadelphia Fed serves the nation's third economic district, which includes Delaware, the eastern region of Pennsylvania and the sourthern portion of New Jersey.

The Fed last raised interest rates on March 25, when it increased its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. At the time, the Fed cited strong demand as one reason behind the preemptive tightening.
The central bank decided to leave interest rates unchanged at the last meeting of its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on May 20. The FOMC meets next on July 1 and 2.
